http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/26/us-wi.text: The "United States will achieve nothing" with its new round of economic sanctions, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday, in another retort from Tehran to Washington's threats of "economic asphyxiation.""With the measures that the government's economic sectors have foreseen, America will not achieve anything with economic pressure at this stage, just as it was unable to achieve anything in the war," Pezeshkian said, according to ISNA news agency."Our principle is understanding and resolving issues through interaction and negotiation, but at the same time, we will stand firm against economic pressures, as we have done so far and will continue to do," he added.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.Iran's leaders have dismissed the impact of the new measures, having already endured decades-long crippling sanctions introduced shortly after the 1979 Islamic revolution.Negotiations between Iran and the US have stalled as the two sides wrangle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.Traffic through the vital waterway — which normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas exports — remains largely paralysed, disrupting global energy markets.Iran has controlled Hormuz since the outbreak of the war on 28 February and has sought to impose fees on vessels transiting the strait.Washington wants the strait to return to its pre-war system of free navigation, and US President Donald Trump has claimed that Washington "has total control" over the waterway.No more military ships in Hormuz?Tehran said on Tuesday it would not allow military vessels to transit through Hormuz under an agreement the Islamic Republic is currently negotiating with Oman, Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state TV late on Tuesday night.The two countries' top diplomats met to discuss managing commercial shipping traffic in the vital waterway and reached an understanding on Tuesday, according to Gharibabadi.“If the understanding becomes binding, no military vessel will be permitted to pass through the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “No military vessel at all.”Gharibabadi did not provide further details about military traffic, but instead described the proposed commercial route through the strait.Traffic into the Persian Gulf from the Gulf of Oman would pass entirely through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman’s territorial waters, he said.The Trump administration told Muscat it opposed parts of the evolving deal, including joint Iranian and Omani management of the exit route from the passage that is critical to global trade.Trump earlier threatened to bomb "the f*** out of" Oman if it “gets in the way”.

https://www.prokerala.com/news/articles/.text: Vilnius : , Sep 8 (IANS) Europe should not give without getting anything in return in any future peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said, stressing that any peace settlement would also involve commitments from Europe. Kallas made the remarks during a visit to Lithuania on Monday (Local time) after US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend in renewed diplomacy to end the war. At a joint press conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius, Kallas was asked whether the weekend talks had brought peace closer and what a possible trilateral summit without an EU seat would mean for Europe's ability to shape the outcome. She said Russia and Ukraine ultimately needed to talk directly to each other. "On the European side, it is clear that we cannot be mediators between Russia and Ukraine. They need to talk to each other. We have always been on the side of Ukraine, so we are not neutral in this situation," Kallas said. She said that any eventual peace agreement would also involve "a lot of asks for Europe," adding that these were not things Europe should give "without getting anything in return." Earlier on Monday, Kallas met Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda and discussed Lithuania's priorities for its upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union, reports Xinhua news agency. Nauseda said Lithuania would focus on European security and defence, EU enlargement, competitiveness, internal security and social resilience during its presidency. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin met with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin on Saturday, with the meeting lasting more than three hours. Witkoff and Kushner then met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday. Additionally, Delegations from Ukraine, the United States and Russia previously held two rounds of talks in Abu Dhabi on January 23-24 and February 4-5, followed by another round in Geneva on February 17-18, in an effort to find a path toward ending the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The trilateral negotiations subsequently stalled and have remained suspended. https://www.politico.eu/article/northern.text: PORTADOWN, Northern Ireland — Hard-liners in Northern Ireland are reviving an age-old dispute rife with bitter symbolism that pits the rights of British Protestants against those of Irish Catholics — and risks the destruction of their supposed unity government. Hundreds of residents of the Garvaghy Road, the main Catholic district in the otherwise staunchly Protestant town of Portadown, near Belfast, stood in the roadway in pouring rain overnight to block a Sunday morning parade by Northern Ireland’s main Protestant brotherhood, the Orange Order — a parade that had been banned since 1998 because of the widespread violence it triggered. The Parades Commission, the British government-appointed group that for decades has adjudicated such zero-sum disputes, stunned Garvaghy Road residents by ruling Friday that a drastically pared-down Orange parade should be allowed to pass through the area Sunday morning. It had refused more than 1,300 previous requests from the group seeking to “finish” the parade it was blocked from completing in 1998. Advertisement Advertisement A series of unprecedented late-night legal challenges followed Saturday, capped by a ruling from Northern Ireland’s senior judge after midnight stating that the courts had no power to overturn the commission’s independent judgment. The scene is now set for a revival of a standoff with no obvious end point — and no apparent way to deliver a “win” for both sides. The Police Service of Northern Ireland deployed several hundred officers to the site. Many of them sat Sunday morning in scores of armored Land Rovers parked on the narrow country lane that separates the would-be Orange marchers on a hilltop church from the Garvaghy Road demonstrators, out of sight beyond houses and hedgerows. The two main parties in Northern Ireland’s cross-community government — revived only two years ago following a lengthy breakdown over Northern Ireland’s peculiar Brexit rules — are lining up on opposite sides of this renewed street battle of wills, raising the political stakes. Sinn Féin, the Irish republican party that represents most Catholics and has grown to become the largest party in Northern Ireland, rallied in force alongside the Garvaghy Road protesters. The Sinn Féin first minister of Northern Ireland’s government, Michelle O’Neill, won cheers as she told the partisan crowd: “The Garvaghy Road residents deserve to live free from sectarian harassment and intimidation.” Advertisement Advertisement “Does anybody think this is a good idea? No right-minded person would make this decision,” said O’Neill, who expressed bewilderment over the Parades Commission’s U-turn. “Why, after 28 years of determinations to block a march down this road, did the Parades Commission think this is the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community?” But Northern Ireland’s main pro-British party, the Democratic Unionists, stood alongside the blocked Orangemen as they waited in hope that the police would enforce the commission’s ruling by pushing the Catholics out of the road. The last time this happened, in 1997, it triggered three nights of Irish republican rioting across Northern Ireland. “It’s a big day for Portadown. Obviously we have had a seismic win within the courts. The law is on our side,” declared the Democratic Unionist MP representing Portadown, Carla Lockhart. She singled out O’Neill for criticism, branding the first minister as a law-breaker leading a mob. “What does it say when you have an absolute rabble, thousands chanting, and our self-proclaimed ‘first minister for all’ leading the chants and standing unlawfully?” Lockhart said. “But these men will continue to stand here,” she said, gesturing to a few dozen Orangemen standing outside the Anglican church, many of them under umbrellas. “They’ve the law on their side. We’ll ensure that the parade is put lawfully down the road.” Advertisement Advertisement Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalist politicians appealed to the British government to intervene. But U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would reverse the commission’s parade ruling only if Northern Ireland’s police commander, Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, recommended another policy U-turn on security grounds. Such a decision would risk the growth of a Protestant counter-protest at the confrontation zone, as happened repeatedly in the 1990s, spurring widespread rioting and isolated killings across Northern Ireland. “There have been big gains made in Northern Ireland and we don’t want to see things go backwards,” Burnham told the BBC. “Obviously (it’s) a challenging situation today. But it’s very important that we work to bring calm.” Burnham’s secretary of state for Northern Ireland, Chris Bryant, said what happens next depends on the judgment of the police chief, not his own. Underscoring the risk of a rapidly deteriorating security situation, he left the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool to fly back to Belfast. “This is primarily a policing matter now,” Bryant told Sky News. He noted that the demonstrators blocking the Garvaghy Road did not have approval from the Parades Commission. “The law states that if you want to mount a protest against a parade, you have to lodge an application with the Parades Commission,” he said. “It means the protest that is going on at the moment is unlawful.” Advertisement Advertisement The Orange Order was founded near Portadown in 1795 to oppose the Catholic community and to celebrate their own side’s 1690 military triumph under the command of King William of Orange. The group mounts thousands of parades annually , concentrated on July 12, the anniversary of that 17th century victory. The Catholic side broadly loathes the parades as demonstrations of Protestant power, and since the 1990s has tried to block any Orange parades that pass near or through their communities. Boutcher, the police commander, issued a carefully worded statement that underscored his desire to avoid physically confronting the Garvaghy Road protesters if possible. Instead, he said officers would collect video and photos to identify those breaking the law — potentially including, though he didn’t specify this, the Sinn Féin leaders — for eventual prosecution. “The policing operation thus far has helped ensure there has been no violence or disorder,” Boutcher said. “We have an evidence gathering operation in place to detect any offenses and will continue to do this throughout today. I appeal to everyone to remain calm and peaceful.” Bracing for potential militant reactions elsewhere to the Portadown standoff, the Northern Irish police this weekend received more than 100 reinforcement officers from Police Scotland .
